1000238.etyen:
From morn (“hello; goodbye”) + a weakened form of da (“then”), literally “morn then”. Linguist Kristin Rygg analyses the expression as a reduction of morgen da (“morning then”) and ultimately an ellipsis of god morgen (“good morning”) followed by da (“then”). Despite its historical connection with a morning greeting, morna functions as a farewell without reference to the time of day.
The fixed expression morna, Jens! is of uncertain origin and is attested at least by 1980, originally also as an exclamation expressing surprise, dismissal or exasperation. It was used politically in reference to

1005102.etyen:
Pseudo-Latinism of uncertain ultimate origin. Probably an alteration of the Latin Catholic Eucharistic formula hoc est enim corpus meum (“for this is my body”), also cited in the shorter form hoc est corpus meum (“this is my body”). The expression is, however, also attested in seventeenth-century English pseudo-Latin conjurers' language as hocus-pocus, and the derivation specifically from the Eucharistic formula is disputed.
Under the Eucharistic interpretation, hoc (“this”) is from *hod (“this”) and *ke (“here”), ultimately involving the Proto-Indo-European particles *gʰe (“discourse particle
